name: The Wilhelminaboom of Hertogplein
access: Free, a public square in the city centre, open at all times
transport: Nijmegen Centraal station, about a 15 minute walk (roughly 970m in a straight line)
verify_notes: A koninginneboom (queen's tree): a lime planted 1 September 1898 to mark Wilhelmina's coronation as Queen of the Netherlands on 6 September 1898, as the centrepiece of Nijmegen's Kroningsfeesten that year. Architect Derk Semmelink designed the ornamental wrought-iron fence around the tree (with small crowns) and, separately, the adjoining Nutsschool building (demolished 1968); the fence still stands on the square today. During the German occupation the crowns were removed from the fence; on 24 July 1948 new crowns, made by students of the Nijmegen ambachtsschool (trade school), were installed with public ceremony. SOURCE CONFLICT, delivered rather than resolved: Dutch Wikipedia's Hertogplein article states plainly 'De oude linde heeft plaatsgemaakt voor een andere boom' (the old lime has made way for another tree), i.e. the tree standing today is a replacement of unstated date, not the 1898 original. The local-history blog woneninnijmegen.blog (2025-04-04, sourced partly from De Gelderlander 1898 archives) makes no mention of any replacement and describes the tree as still standing, without saying explicitly whether it is the same physical specimen. The LRMB register's own planted_band for this entry is 1880-1890, which predates the 1898 planting date both other sources give for the coronation tree, a further inconsistency the register does not explain (register bands are rough estimates, not always tree-specific plaques). Net effect: do not state an age with confidence. The remarkable and verifiable thing about this tree is the 128-year-old civic story around it (the coronation planting, the crown fence, its wartime and postwar restoration), not a specific ring count. Species: no source names the exact Tilia species/cultivar; register's species field is blank. Worth a page question asking a reader with local knowledge whether this is verifiably the 1898 original or its successor.

name: The Beverboom of Park Leeuwenstein
species: Magnolia (Magnolia sp., exact species not confirmed)
access: Free, public municipal park (Park Leeuwenstein), open at all times per the register (owner_category gemeente, visitable=ja); exact sightline to the trunk not itself confirmed this pass (register's own visible field is 'onbekend')
transport: Roughly 2.9km from Nijmegen city centre; no specific bus stop or walk time checked this pass, flagged as approximate
verify_notes: LRMB register nr 1680530, 'Beverboom Park Leeuwenstein, Nijmegen', status 3/monumentaal, reason 'dendrologisch' (registered for being a dendrologically notable specimen rather than for age or civic history), single tree (n_trees=1), tree-level coordinates, planted_band 1880-1890, owner gemeente, visitable=ja, visible=onbekend. Park Leeuwenstein is the surviving garden of the demolished Villa Leeuwenstein (built mid-19th century, demolished 1958 in a dilapidated state), a small park known for exotic specimen trees planted alongside the villa in the second half of the 19th century. SPECIES CAUTION: 'beverboom' is the generic old Dutch name once used for the Magnolia genus and specifically for Magnolia virginiana ('de enige echte beverboom', per a directly-fetched dendrology-society article, dendrologie.nl); a WebSearch AI summary (not independently verified by fetching the source page, so treated as a lead per the search-summary rule) suggested the register entry might correspond to a Magnolia acuminata (Komkommermagnolia) that monumentaltrees.com separately lists for this park, but the directly-fetched dendrology source does NOT confirm 'beverboom' is used for M. acuminata, so that identification is NOT treated as established. A directly-fetched local-history blog post (woneninnijmegen.blog, dated 2023-08-16) lists a 'Komkommermagnolia' among the park's current special trees, present tense, as of August 2023, distinct from '2 grootste bomen' (2 largest trees) it says were lost in recent years (see the blocked mammoetboom entry, same park). This is corroborating but NOT a location-matched confirmation that the blog's Komkommermagnolia and the register's coordinate-pinned Beverboom are the same individual specimen; both are magnolias in the same small park but the match is inferential. DELIVERED FLAGGED rather than dropped to leads because there is no evidence against the tree (unlike its neighbour, no death signal found for this one), the register gives a genuine tree-level pin, and BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's rule is to deliver thin-but-not-contradicted alive-evidence flagged rather than withhold it. Age: register planted_band 1880-1890 is the only age evidence; no growth-rate/girth basis available (no girth recorded). Page should ask the reader to confirm the exact species (photograph of the flower would settle it: M. acuminata flowers are greenish-yellow and appear after leaves in late spring; M. virginiana flowers are creamy-white and fragrant in early summer). monumentaltrees.com itself could not be fetched to check (403 to both curl with browser UA and WebFetch, matches the known blocklist pattern for this host; no Wayback snapshot exists for its Park Leeuwenstein pages, checked via the archive.org availability API, empty result).
